lessons.title: Place value and rounding
lessons.summary: Use powers of ten to change a number and round measurements to a stated precision.
lessons.objective: Use powers of ten to change a number and round measurements to a stated precision.
lessons.before: Put each digit in a place-value column. A digit moves one place for each factor of ten.
lessons.ideas:
One column to the left makes a digit worth ten times as much. Keep a zero in a column if no digit fills it.

Divide by ten by moving each digit one column to the right in a place-value chart.

If the next digit is 0 to 4, keep the last digit. If it is 5 to 9, increase the last digit and carry if needed.
lessons.method:
Use the power of 10 to count the number of moves before writing the answer.

For a positive starting value, check the quotient is smaller when dividing by a power of ten greater than one.

Keep a final zero if it shows the number of decimal places requested.
mistakes: Moving the decimal point can hide what changes. Track the value of the digits in their columns.
Two zeros in 100 mean two places, even if the original number already contains zeros.
Do the rounding once. Rounding to two places and then to one place can give a different answer.

lessons.title: Calculating with signed integers
lessons.summary: Estimate and use the four operations with positive and negative whole numbers.
lessons.objective: Estimate and use the four operations with positive and negative whole numbers.
lessons.before: Start at the first number. The sign of the number you add gives the direction.
lessons.ideas:
Add a positive by moving right. Add a negative by moving left.

To subtract an integer, add its opposite. For example, \(2-(-3)=2+3=5\).

For multiplication and division, equal signs give a positive answer and different signs give a negative answer.
lessons.method:
Estimate with nearby signed multiples of ten.

Rewrite subtraction as addition of the opposite before using a number line.

Predict the sign before calculating the size.
mistakes: The first number sets the start point. Keep its sign.
Two minus signs only become plus when you actually subtract a negative number.
A negative answer in a temperature problem often describes a drop. The size of the drop is positive.

examples.title: Temperature changes
examples.question:
A freezer drops by 32 degrees per hour for 2 hours.

  1. What is the total signed change?

    [2]

  2. Divide your total signed change by 2 to check the signed change per hour.

    [2]

  3. Write a signed division that gives the same answer as dividing 64 by 2.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Each hour changes the temperature by \(-32\) degrees.

Use \(2\times -32\).

\(-64\) degrees.

(b) Divide the negative total, -64, by the positive time, 2.

The signs differ, so the quotient is negative.

\(-32\) degrees per hour.

(c) Both numbers can be negative because a negative divided by a negative is positive.

\(-64\) divided by \(-2\) gives \(32\).

lessons.title: Powers, roots and calculation order
lessons.summary: Read square and cube notation and work out expressions in the correct order.
lessons.objective: Read square and cube notation and work out expressions in the correct order.
lessons.before: An expression is a set of instructions. Group with brackets when you want an operation to happen first.
lessons.ideas:
Work inside brackets first. Then work out powers, then multiply or divide from left to right, then add or subtract from left to right.

\(6^2=6\times6=36\) and \(\sqrt{36}=6\). The square root symbol asks for the non-negative root.

\(4^3=4\times4\times4=64\) and \(\sqrt[3]{64}=4\).
lessons.method:
Write each line of working with the same value as the previous line.

Check a positive square root by squaring it.

Cube your answer to check a cube root.
mistakes: A multiplication still comes before an addition when you read it second.
Squaring means multiplying a number by itself, not multiplying it by two.
Use three equal factors to make a cube. Adding the edges does not count all the blocks.

examples.title: Compare two calculations
examples.question:
The same three numbers, 5, 2 and 5, appear in two calculations.

  1. Work out \(5+2\times 5^2\).

    [2]

  2. Work out \((5+2)\times 5^2\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Calculate 5 squared first. It is 25.

Multiply 2 by 25, then add 5.

\(55\).

(b) Work out the bracket: 7.

Multiply that by 25.

\(175\).

examples.title: Square tiles
examples.question:
A square sits on a board next to a row of 2 loose tiles. The square has area 324 square units.

  1. What is the side length of the square?

    [2]

  2. How many tiles are used, including the loose tiles, if each covers one square unit?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Find the positive number that gives 324 when multiplied by itself.

18 squared is 324.

\(18\).

(b) The square takes 324 tiles.

Add the 2 loose tiles.

\(326\).

examples.title: A cube made of small blocks
examples.question:
A solid cube contains 125 small unit cubes. A second cube has an edge 1 units longer.

  1. How long is each edge of the first cube?

    [2]

  2. How many blocks make the second cube?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) A cube with edge 5 has 5 lots of 5 by 5.

\(5^3\) is \(125\).

\(5\) units.

(b) The edge is 6 units.

Multiply 6 by itself three times.

\(216\).

lessons.title: Factors, multiples and divisibility
lessons.summary: Find common factors and multiples and test divisibility of larger whole numbers.
lessons.objective: Find common factors and multiples and test divisibility of larger whole numbers.
lessons.before: Two totals can be split into the same number of equal groups only when that group count divides both totals exactly.
lessons.ideas:
List or pair factors of each number. The highest common factor is the greatest value on both lists.

A least common multiple is the smallest positive value in both lists of multiples.

Check the ones digit for 2, 5 and 10. Add the digits for divisibility by 3 or 9. Check the last two digits for divisibility by 4.
lessons.method:
Test a proposed common factor by dividing both numbers.

Check that both periods divide your time gap exactly.

Show the particular fact your test uses.
mistakes: The smaller total is only the highest common factor if it divides the larger total exactly.
The product of both periods is a common multiple, but there may be a smaller one.
Adding digits tests 3 and 9. It does not test an arbitrary divisor.

examples.title: Identical activity packs
examples.question:
A club has 10 pencils and 15 stickers. It uses all the items to make identical packs.

  1. Find the greatest possible number of packs.

    [2]

  2. How many stickers go into each of these packs?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The number of packs must divide both 10 and 15 exactly.

The greatest shared divisor is 5.

\(5\).

(b) Share 15 stickers among 5 packs.

\(3\).

examples.title: Two flashing lights
examples.question:
An amber light flashes every 24 seconds and a blue light every 18 seconds. Both flash at second 1.

  1. How many seconds after second 1 will both first flash at the same time?

    [2]

  2. At which clock second does this happen?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Look for a positive number in both the 24 and 18 times tables.

The first match is 72.

\(72\) seconds.

(b) Add the interval 72 to the start time 1.

\(73\) seconds.

examples.title: Testing factors of a larger number
examples.question:
A store has 980 small clips. Different organisers are sold in trays of 7, 10, 11 and 12.

  1. How many trays of 7 can be filled exactly using all the clips?

    [2]

  2. Use a divisibility test to decide whether trays of 10 can use all the clips.

    [2]

  3. Give another factor of the number greater than 1.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Divide 980 by 7.

Check by multiplying 140 by 7.

\(140\).

(b) The ones digit of 980 is 0.

A whole number is divisible by 10 exactly when the ones digit is 0.

Yes, because the ones digit is 0.

(c) The multiplication \(140\times 7\) gives 980.

For example, 140 is also a factor.
